query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding a modest amount of interstitial oxygen to a Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high‐entropy alloy will enhance its glass‐forming ability compared to the undoped base alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A fully crystalline Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high‐entropy alloy prepared via arc melting and cast into a water‐cooled copper mold.
generation.intervention: Interstitial oxygen doping to form an oxygen-doped composition, for example (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2.
generation.conditions: Standard arc-melting conditions with controlled oxygen incorporation and comparable cooling rates between doped and undoped alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of ordered oxygen complexes (OOCs) within the bcc lattice.
generation.mechanism: Interstitial oxygen atoms form ordered complexes that locally disturb atomic configurations and introduce topological frustration. This hinders atomic rearrangements necessary for crystallization during rapid cooling, thereby promoting glass formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The oxygen-doped HEA will exhibit a higher resistance to crystallization during cooling, evidenced by a broader undercooled liquid stability range and a delay in the onset of crystallization exotherms relative to the undoped alloy.
generation.baseline: The undoped Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA, which under identical processing conditions crystallizes more readily.
generation.boundary: The enhancement is anticipated only for moderate oxygen doping levels (around 2% interstitial oxygen), and effects may be sensitive to cooling rate; too high an oxygen content or vastly different processing conditions might negate the beneficial impact.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvement in glass forming ability is uncertain and needs to be quantified, as the current evidence indirectly supports the role of interstitial oxygen in modifying lattice dynamics but does not directly measure glass formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi alloy: one undoped and one doped with approximately 2% interstitial oxygen (targeting the (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 composition) using identical arc-melting and casting methods into water-cooled copper molds. Systematically vary the cooling rates.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess the fraction of amorphous versus crystalline phases
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the onset temperature and exothermic peak associated with crystallization
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to analyze local structure and confirm the presence of ordered oxygen complexes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped alloy does not demonstrate a measurable increase in the amorphous fraction (or exhibit a delayed crystallization exotherm) compared to the undoped alloy under controlled cooling conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
